purpose: Goserelin is used to treat certain hormone-sensitive cancers, including prostate cancer in men and breast cancer in women. It is also used to treat endometriosis and uterine fibroids in women. By lowering certain hormone levels in your body, it helps slow or stop the growth of these conditions.
how_it_works: Your body normally makes hormones like testosterone and estrogen that can fuel certain cancers or conditions. Goserelin works by signaling your brain to stop producing the hormones that trigger testosterone or estrogen production. Think of it like turning down a thermostat — it lowers those hormone levels so they can no longer feed the problem.
common_side_effects: Hot flashes or sweats, decreased sex drive, erectile problems in men, vaginal dryness or irregular periods in women, mood changes, tiredness, headaches, bone or joint pain, and injection site reactions like redness or bruising where the shot is given.
warnings: Long-term use can weaken your bones, so your doctor may check your bone density and recommend calcium or vitamin D. It can cause mood changes or depression, so tell your doctor if you feel very low. Men with prostate cancer may notice a brief worsening of symptoms in the first few weeks. Do not use if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, as it can harm the baby. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take.
typical_dosing: Goserelin is given as a small implant injected just under the skin of the abdomen (belly area) by a healthcare provider. The most common doses are 3.6 mg once every 4 weeks, or 10.8 mg once every 12 weeks, depending on your condition. You do not take it as a pill — your doctor or nurse gives you the injection at each visit.
